title: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
gist: Former AlphaGo team member Thore Graepel argues LLMs, even with chain of thought, are System 1 next-token predictors lacking an explicit, auditable epistemic state, and that trustworthy AI for science and medicine needs AlphaGo-style search over a belief state with an independent verifier.

insights.claim: AlphaGo's move 37 against Lee Sedol in March 2016 was chosen by its search machinery rather than by machine intuition; its policy network rated the move at roughly a 1-in-10,000 chance of being played by an expert human.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Creative AI output came from explicit search over futures, not from pattern matching alone.
insights.locator: AlphaGo is made up of two systems

insights.claim: AlphaGo explicitly built and searched a game tree with thousands of branches, each a possible future annotated with neural-network judgments, and updated it as reasoning progressed before synthesizing a move.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: The game tree is a concrete template for an inspectable reasoning state in AI systems.
insights.locator: AlphaGo maintains a record of what it knows

insights.claim: Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997 by looking six to eight moves ahead and evaluating 200 million positions per second with human hard-coded rules, whereas Go is far too complex for that brute-force approach.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Shows that Go-level progress required learned intuition combined with search, a different paradigm from brute force.

insights.claim: AlphaGo is a machine analogue of Kahneman's System 1 and System 2: neural networks supplied hunches and search supplied deliberation, and neither half works alone.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for judging whether an AI architecture pairs intuition with deliberation.
insights.quote: As in human cognition, neither half works alone.
insights.locator: A well-known theory in the behavioral sciences

themes.theme: Why LLMs do not truly reason

insights.claim: Large language models operate as System 1: they pick the next token repeatedly, giving fast associative pattern completion across nearly every subject people write about.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Frames LLM capability limits in terms of architecture, not scale.

insights.claim: Chain-of-thought gains are real, above all in mathematics and coding, but they add no separate reasoning mechanism because the intermediate steps are produced by the same next-token prediction run for longer.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Reasoning-model improvements may hit a ceiling if they only extend the same mechanism.
insights.locator: The apparent solution was to make models that deliberate

insights.claim: LLMs typically keep no explicit, persistent, inspectable epistemic state, meaning no ledger of hypotheses, confidence, evidence weighed, and open questions that is revised as new information arrives.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Missing capability that would be a differentiator for any lab or startup that builds it.

insights.claim: In LLMs, knowledge and the reasoning that manipulates it are interwoven in the neural network weights, with no independent, explicitly represented set of beliefs.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Makes auditing and targeted correction of model beliefs hard.
insights.locator: Second, they lack a clean separation

insights.claim: Research has shown that chatbots often concoct chains of thought after the fact, reaching an answer by one route but reporting another, so displayed reasoning may not reflect the real process.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Undermines trust in displayed reasoning traces as an audit tool in regulated or high-stakes deployments.
insights.locator: Third, while the chains of thought

insights.claim: In medicine, engineering and scientific research it matters how a system reaches a conclusion, because errors must be traced to faulty reasoning, invalid evidence or wrong assumptions.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Auditability is a likely adoption gate for AI in high-stakes sectors.
insights.locator: This is a problem because in the high-stakes applications

insights.claim: The author left Google DeepMind to pursue a new approach to machine reasoning based on AlphaGo's architecture.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Signals talent movement toward reasoning-centric research outside big labs.
insights.locator: This is why I recently left my position

insights.claim: A general reasoning system should maintain an epistemic state of what is settled, doubted, ruled out and open, and reason as a sequence of moves that change that state, including choosing the next question, calculation or experiment.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Concrete design spec to watch for in next-generation AI research agents.

insights.claim: An independent component must evaluate each reasoning move by how much it resolves uncertainty and update beliefs only when evidence backs the change, letting the system accumulate certified knowledge and improve its reasoning policy from experience.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: A verifier separate from the generator is the key architectural idea to track.
insights.locator: Most important, to keep the system honest

insights.claim: Recent LLM advances make open-world reasoning tractable because LLMs can propose approaches given known facts and resources, use tools via APIs or code, and assess whether evidence supports a claim.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: LLMs become components inside larger reasoning systems rather than the whole system.

insights.claim: Open-world reasoning is harder than Go or chess because the state is only partially known, actions are large and variable, and consequences are stochastic or unknown.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Caveat on how directly game-AI success transfers to real-world domains.

insights.claim: Making System 1 bigger will not yield trustworthy machine intelligence, because scale sharpens intuition without making it more deliberative.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Counters the view that scaling alone gets to reliable AI; favors architecture-focused bets.
insights.quote: I do not think we reach trustworthy machine intelligence by making system 1 bigger.
insights.locator: I do not think we reach trustworthy

insights.claim: Genuinely novel, creative insights in drug discovery, materials, climate and diagnosis will come only from systems whose conclusions arise from an auditable sequence of evidence, inference and belief revision.
insights.speaker: Thore Graepel
insights.so_what: Points to science-oriented AI as where reasoning architectures would pay off.
